# Runix Lab

> Runix Lab is rebuilding Unix for AI (its motto: "Rebuild AI Unix"; the name is Rebuild +
> Unix): an efficient, stable,
> enterprise-grade AI operating system in five layers, each one a product a team can use
> on its own: infrastructure (Runix FS, an AI-native file system over object
> storage), data (Runix Data, domain training and evaluation data, and Runix Pipeline, the
> data tooling), models (Runix Models, fine-tuning and dedicated serving of open-weight
> models), gateway (Runix Router, one OpenAI-compatible API in front of many model
> providers) and agents (Runix Code and Runix Comic, independent agents for their domains, each with its own harness). Operated by Runix AI Inc, a
> company incorporated in Wyoming, United States. Router, FS, Data and Models are in early
> access: accounts and engagements are set up on request rather than through self-serve
> signup.

## The idea

Unix lasted on a few ideas, and each layer rebuilds one of them for AI: everything is a
file (Runix FS), small tools joined by pipes (Runix Data and Runix Pipeline), a kernel
that does the work (Runix Models), one call interface (Runix Router), and userland on top:
agents and the harnesses that run them (Runix Code and Runix Comic). The aims are efficiency, stability and what an enterprise
needs to buy it: contracts, key custody and deployment into its own cloud account.

## The stack

Five layers, top to bottom as the home page draws them, standing on the customer's own
compute (GPUs, power and cloud capacity), which Runix Lab does not sell:

- Layer 5, Agents: Runix Code, Runix Comic (independent domain agents and their harnesses)
- Layer 4, Gateway: Runix Router
- Layer 3, Models: Runix Models
- Layer 2, Data: Runix Data, Runix Pipeline (domains: code, the focus; finance;
  cybersecurity; legal; embodied AI; AI for Science)
- Layer 1, Infrastructure: Runix FS

## Products

Seven products at different stages. The statuses below are literal.

- **Runix Router** — *status: early access, running traffic today.* One OpenAI-compatible
  endpoint across many providers, positioned on security, compliance and performance:
  central key custody, per-key limits and quotas, request-level audit trail, contracts and
  written data terms, automatic failover between providers with streaming preserved, and
  routing by cost, health and configuration. Hosted API, billed on usage.
  https://runixcloud.io/router
  Models catalogue, every model at its vendor's public list price: https://runixcloud.io/router-models
- **Runix FS** — *status: early access, launched September 2026.* An AI-native file system:
  a POSIX file system (FUSE) and a memory/SSD/HDD distributed cache in front of
  S3-compatible object storage, with a Hadoop-compatible client,
  Java/Python/Rust SDKs and a Kubernetes CSI driver. File paths map one-to-one to object
  keys, so data in the bucket stays independently readable; a mount either keeps the bucket
  as the source of truth (cache mode, for read-heavy data) or completes writes in Runix FS
  first and syncs them to the bucket in the background (file-system mode). Built on Curvine
  (Apache 2.0, a CNCF Sandbox project); Runix deploys it into the customer's own cloud
  account and supports it under contract. Priced per deployment during early access.
  https://runixcloud.io/fs
- **Runix Models** — *status: early access, by engagement.* Fine-tuning and dedicated
  serving of small and open-weight models (for example Qwen, Llama, Mistral, Gemma and
  DeepSeek, with the licence checked against the use case first): supervised fine-tuning,
  LoRA and QLoRA, preference tuning (DPO), evaluation against the model a team runs today,
  and single-tenant serving in the customer's cloud account or on capacity arranged per
  engagement, behind an OpenAI-compatible API that can sit behind Runix Router. Priced per
  engagement. https://runixcloud.io/models
- **Runix Data** — *status: early access, by engagement.* Training and evaluation data in six
  domains: code (the focus: repository and task data for code models and coding agents,
  with each task verified by running its tests in a clean container), finance,
  cybersecurity, legal, embodied AI, and AI for Science (limited to biological data:
  antibody and protein records). Every delivery carries per-record provenance and licence,
  a quality report, personal data masked (failing closed) and evaluation data split from
  training data by source. Priced per project or volume. https://runixcloud.io/data
- **Runix Pipeline** — *status: in development with design partners.* The tooling behind
  Runix Data, being built for teams to run themselves. Managed data preparation for AI: ingestion, cleaning, three tiers of deduplication, schema-validated
  LLM extraction, PII masking that fails closed, and a quality report with every delivery.
  Scoped and priced per project or volume. https://runixcloud.io/pipeline
- **Runix Code** — *status: in development, waitlist open.* An AI coding agent being built
  for teams: codebase-aware completion and chat, agentic multi-file tasks that land as
  reviewable diffs, and team controls (seats, usage attribution, model routing policies,
  written data terms). Not generally available. https://runixcloud.io/code
- **Runix Comic** — *status: in development, waitlist open.* An end-to-end AI studio for
  comic dramas being built to cover pre-production (scripts, consistent characters,
  storyboards), production (styled panels, motion, voice-over, subtitles) and publishing
  (export, multi-platform distribution, promotional assets). Not generally available.
  https://runixcloud.io/comic

## Solutions, by team

The other way in, beside the stack: six kinds of team, the problem each usually arrives
with, the products that fit and how work starts. Every product is also sold on its own.
Hub: https://runixcloud.io/solutions

- Platform teams (Router first; FS where data lives in object storage): https://runixcloud.io/for-platform-teams
- Model teams (Data, Pipeline, Models, FS): https://runixcloud.io/for-model-teams
- Engineering organisations (Code, in development; Router for policy and attribution): https://runixcloud.io/for-engineering-orgs
- Studios and creators (Comic, in development; Router optional): https://runixcloud.io/for-studios
- Regulated industries (Router's written terms; Data's finance, legal and cybersecurity domains; single-tenant serving): https://runixcloud.io/for-regulated-industries
- Research labs (FS for datasets in buckets; Data's AI for Science and embodied AI domains; Models): https://runixcloud.io/for-research-labs

## The Agents layer, by domain

The top layer is presented by professional domain. Two agents exist today, both in
development with waitlists open: software engineering (Runix Code) and media and
entertainment (Runix Comic). The domains the Data layer already has rules for (finance,
cybersecurity, legal, AI for Science) are named as candidates; no agent is announced for
them. https://runixcloud.io/agents

## Roadmap

Where each product is, drawn from the same product definitions as the home page, what
general availability adds (a complete API reference, a published service level for Router,
self-serve signup and checkout), and what has shipped with the date. No dates are published
for anything forward-looking. https://runixcloud.io/roadmap

## Facts a buyer usually asks for

- Legal entity: Runix AI Inc, Wyoming, United States.
- Contracting: MSA and DPA on request, reviewed per engagement; an order form takes
  precedence over the standard Terms.
- Billing: USD, usage-based (per token or per request, by model), itemised statements,
  prepaid draw-down or invoiced. There is no published rate card; quotes are per workload.
- Data handling: customer prompt and response content is not used to train models and is
  not sold. The one exception is Runix Models, where data a customer provides trains the
  model that customer asked for, as Section 5 of the Terms of Service sets out. Operational metadata (usage counts, latency, error codes) is kept to run
  billing, reliability and support. Details in the Privacy Policy and Security page.
- Certifications: none are claimed. Runix does not assert SOC 2, ISO 27001 or PCI status.
- Support: replies within one business day, contact@runixcloud.io.

## Writing

All 58 posts, newest first. Descriptions are the pages' own.

- [Domain-specific AI agents: why agents are built one profession at a time](https://runixcloud.io/blog/ai-agents-by-domain) — Why AI agents are built per profession: the domain supplies the tools, the data rules, the evaluation and the review gate, and a generic agent lacks all four.
- [Auto routing versus a pinned model id: choosing an LLM routing policy](https://runixcloud.io/blog/auto-routing-versus-a-pinned-model-id) — Two routing policies behind one endpoint: auto, chosen by cost and health, or a pinned model id. When each is right, and what to log to keep both honest.
- [Exact, near and semantic: why near-duplicate detection for training data needs all three](https://runixcloud.io/blog/deduplication-exact-near-semantic) — Exact hashing, MinHash and embeddings each catch a different kind of duplicate. What each misses and costs, and how duplicates inflate evaluation scores.
- [Evaluate coding agents on your own repository, not on a leaderboard](https://runixcloud.io/blog/evaluate-a-coding-agent-on-your-own-repository) — Leaderboard scores do not transfer to your codebase. How to build a task set from closed issues with fail-to-pass tests, and what to measure beyond pass rate.
- [How to evaluate a fine-tuned LLM against the model you run today](https://runixcloud.io/blog/evaluate-the-tuned-model-against-your-baseline) — Held-out sets, task metrics versus generic benchmarks, regression checks on what you did not tune, contamination, and when a tuned model is ready to ship.
- [Fine-tuning vs RAG vs prompting: a decision guide by failure mode](https://runixcloud.io/blog/fine-tune-prompt-or-retrieve) — When a prompt is enough, when retrieval fixes a knowledge or freshness gap, when fine-tuning is the right tool, and how the failure mode tells you which one.
- [FUSE, CSI or SDK: three ways to mount object storage in Kubernetes for ML workloads](https://runixcloud.io/blog/fuse-csi-or-sdk-mounting-object-storage-for-ml) — FUSE mount, CSI driver or SDK: three ways to get a bucket into ML pods on Kubernetes, what each changes in your code, how each fails, and when to pick which.
- [How to read an LLM price list](https://runixcloud.io/blog/how-to-read-an-llm-price-list) — Units, cached input, batch and tiered rates, context bands and media pricing: how to read a vendor's LLM price list and record a dated baseline to compare on.
- [How to read an open-weight model licence before you fine-tune it](https://runixcloud.io/blog/how-to-read-an-open-weight-model-licence) — The clauses that decide whether you can fine-tune and ship an open-weight model: use restrictions, attribution, user thresholds, redistribution and patents.
- [Keeping GPUs fed: where the GPU data loading bottleneck comes from](https://runixcloud.io/blog/keeping-gpus-fed-data-loading-bottleneck) — How input pipelines starve accelerators: dataloader workers, random reads, IOPS versus throughput, object storage latency, and honest utilisation metrics.
- [Turning an LLM bill into a policy: budgets per team and per feature](https://runixcloud.io/blog/llm-budgets-per-team-and-per-feature) — Turning an LLM bill into enforceable policy: per-key quotas, allowed models, hard stops versus alerts, what happens at the limit, and how retries draw on it.
- [LoRA vs QLoRA vs full fine-tuning: what each one changes in the weights](https://runixcloud.io/blog/lora-qlora-and-full-fine-tuning) — What LoRA and QLoRA change in the weights, the memory and quality trade-offs, merging versus adapter serving, and when full fine-tuning is still warranted.
- [A multi-tier cache for AI training data: what goes where](https://runixcloud.io/blog/multi-tier-cache-for-ai-training-data) — Memory, SSD and HDD tiers for training data: what goes where, how eviction and warming work, page cache or distributed cache, and when caching is pointless.
- [Object storage is not a file system, and what POSIX on object storage adds](https://runixcloud.io/blog/object-storage-is-not-a-file-system) — Object storage has no rename, no partial writes and no directories. What a POSIX layer over a bucket has to add, and what it still cannot promise.
- [PII masking for training data that fails closed: detect, mask, measure, hold back](https://runixcloud.io/blog/pii-masking-that-fails-closed) — Pattern, NER and context detection, masking versus pseudonymisation versus dropping, why uncleared records are held back, and how to measure recall honestly.
- [DPO fine-tuning explained: what preference tuning changes and what it cannot](https://runixcloud.io/blog/preference-tuning-with-dpo-explained) — How DPO fine-tuning learns from chosen and rejected pairs without a reward model, where preference tuning helps and where it cannot, and the data pitfalls.
- [Reviewable by default: why an agent's changes should land as diffs](https://runixcloud.io/blog/reviewable-by-default-agent-changes-as-diffs) — Agent output should land as a diff a person can review, not a silent write. Blast radius, attribution, tests as the gate, and how reviewing an agent differs.
- [Single-tenant model serving explained: what a dedicated LLM inference endpoint changes](https://runixcloud.io/blog/single-tenant-model-serving-explained) — What single-tenant serving means beside a shared endpoint: isolation, latency under your own load, capacity planning, quantised variants and operations.
- [The small files problem in machine learning: millions of samples, one metadata bill](https://runixcloud.io/blog/small-files-problem-in-ml-training) — Why millions of small samples cost more than their bytes: per-object overhead, listing, metadata pressure, and packing formats versus a metadata service.
- [Split by source, not by row: how benchmark contamination reaches your own evaluation set](https://runixcloud.io/blog/split-by-source-not-by-row) — Row splits put near-duplicates on both sides of an evaluation. Why to split by repository, document or entity, and how to decontaminate and report overlap.
- [The harness: what actually runs an AI agent](https://runixcloud.io/blog/the-harness-what-runs-an-ai-agent) — An agent harness is the runtime around a model: tools, permissions, context, budgets and logs. Why it, not the model, decides if an agent is safe to run.
- [Training data provenance: what every record should carry, and why a README is not proof](https://runixcloud.io/blog/training-data-provenance-and-licence) — What a provenance entry should carry per record, from source and retrieval date to an SPDX licence identifier, and why a detected licence beats a README.
- [Fail-to-pass and pass-to-pass tests in clean containers: what makes a coding task valid](https://runixcloud.io/blog/verified-coding-tasks-fail-to-pass) — Fail-to-pass and pass-to-pass tests, clean containers, why a task whose tests pass without the patch is invalid, and what SWE-bench Verified screened for.
- [What a data quality report should contain, and how to read one sceptically](https://runixcloud.io/blog/what-a-data-quality-report-should-contain) — What a data quality report should state about coverage, duplication, extraction confidence, drops and licences, and how a buyer reads one sceptically.
- [What is a coding agent? From autocomplete to pull requests](https://runixcloud.io/blog/what-is-a-coding-agent) — A coding agent reads a repository, plans, edits files, runs tests and revises until they pass. What separates it from an assistant, and what it is not.
- [When the bucket is the truth: AI file system cache mode versus file-system mode](https://runixcloud.io/blog/when-the-bucket-is-the-truth-two-mount-modes) — Cache mode and fs mode: what each guarantees about the bucket behind an AI file system, which workloads fit which, and what to ask a vendor about truth.
- [Why five layers: how Runix drew its AI infrastructure stack](https://runixcloud.io/blog/why-five-layers) — How Runix drew five layers over the customer's own compute, which Unix idea each layer rebuilds, why each must work alone, and what the layered view omits.
- [Rebuild AI Unix: why Runix Lab is building an operating system for AI](https://runixcloud.io/blog/rebuild-ai-unix) — Unix lasted on a few ideas: files, pipes, a kernel, one call interface. Runix Lab is rebuilding them for enterprise AI, in five layers.
- [Introducing Runix FS: an AI file system for object storage](https://runixcloud.io/blog/introducing-runix-fs) — Runix FS puts a POSIX file system and a multi-tier cache in front of object storage. Why the layer is missing, what it is built on, and how early access works.
- [One key can drain a shared quota pool](https://runixcloud.io/blog/per-key-llm-quotas) — A shared quota pool with no per-key ceiling is first-come-first-served — one client's batch job empties it. Why runway beats balance as an alert threshold.
- [The security review an LLM gateway should survive](https://runixcloud.io/blog/llm-gateway-security-review) — Eight questions a security review should ask any LLM gateway — key custody, logging, retention, tenant isolation, egress — and what good answers look like.
- [Your LLM traffic needs a retry budget, not a retry count](https://runixcloud.io/blog/llm-retry-budget) — Retries multiply cost and load exactly when a provider is struggling. What a retry budget is, which errors deserve one, and how failover changes the arithmetic.
- [Why your LLM bill doesn't match the price list](https://runixcloud.io/blog/why-your-llm-bill-doesnt-match-the-price-list) — Cache multipliers, injected prompts, tokenizer changes, tiered rates: the mechanics behind a surprising token bill, and how to reconcile one request by hand.
- [How to tell whether a model change made things worse](https://runixcloud.io/blog/did-the-model-change-make-it-worse) — Output varies run to run, so a quality regression does not announce itself. Four signals that move before anyone files a ticket.
- [How long should an LLM request be allowed to take?](https://runixcloud.io/blog/how-long-should-an-llm-request-wait) — Standard HTTP timeout advice is wrong for model traffic. Which timeout to set, where each one belongs, and why stacked timeouts cause the outage.
- [What to settle before an LLM feature carries real traffic](https://runixcloud.io/blog/llm-feature-pre-launch-checklist) — Twelve decisions that are cheap before launch and expensive after: cost ceilings, timeouts, failover, what you log, and how you roll back.
- [Migrating to a gateway without a maintenance window](https://runixcloud.io/blog/migrating-to-an-llm-gateway-without-downtime) — Shadow, then a percentage, then a cutover you can reverse in one config change — and the three things about LLM traffic the usual playbook does not cover.
- [Your model id has an expiry date](https://runixcloud.io/blog/model-deprecation-without-a-redeploy) — Providers retire model versions on a published schedule. If the id is a string literal in your code, their calendar is your deploy calendar.
- ["OpenAI-compatible" is a surface, not a contract](https://runixcloud.io/blog/what-openai-compatible-actually-means) — Compatibility claims cover the endpoint shape, rarely the details that break you: ignored parameters, missing usage, streaming that ends wrong. How to test one.
- [Where your prompts actually go](https://runixcloud.io/blog/where-your-prompts-actually-go) — Every security review opens with this and most teams cannot answer it. How to trace the path text takes through an LLM integration, hop by hop.
- [Comic Drama vs Webtoon vs Motion Comic, Explained](https://runixcloud.io/blog/comic-drama-vs-webtoon-vs-motion-comic) — Three overlapping formats for drawn stories: how webtoons, motion comics and comic dramas differ in production, distribution and audience — and which to make.
- [How to Make a Comic Drama with AI: Script to Screen](https://runixcloud.io/blog/how-to-make-a-comic-drama-with-ai) — The full AI comic drama production line: script and characters, storyboards, styled panels, motion, voice and publishing — and where tools still fall short.
- [LLM Router vs LLM Gateway: What's the Difference?](https://runixcloud.io/blog/llm-router-vs-llm-gateway) — The two names describe overlapping tools. What routing and gateway features actually do, when the difference matters, and how to choose on capabilities.
- [12 Data Questions to Ask an AI Vendor](https://runixcloud.io/blog/ai-vendor-data-questions) — The data-handling questions that decide an AI procurement review, what a good answer sounds like, and which vague replies should stop the process.
- [Build or Buy an LLM Gateway: An Honest Comparison](https://runixcloud.io/blog/build-vs-buy-llm-gateway) — The first version of a gateway is a weekend. The parts that take a year are retry budgets, streaming failover, cost accounting and being on call for all of it.
- [LLM Provider Keys: Scope, Rotation and Blast Radius](https://runixcloud.io/blog/llm-api-key-management) — Provider keys spread through repos, CI and notebooks. How to scope and rotate them, and why a compromised LLM key is a billing incident as well as a data one.
- [Per-Team LLM Cost Attribution That Survives Audit](https://runixcloud.io/blog/llm-cost-attribution) — Provider invoices arrive as one number. How to attach cost to a team, feature and request at call time, and why reconstructing it later never works.
- [What to Log for LLM Traffic, and What Not To](https://runixcloud.io/blog/llm-observability) — Status codes and latency miss the failures that matter for LLM traffic. The signals worth recording, the fields to redact, and the alerts worth waking up for.
- [Surviving LLM Rate Limits: 429s, Budgets and Queues](https://runixcloud.io/blog/llm-rate-limits) — Why provider rate limits bite in bursts, how RPM, TPM and concurrency interact, and the queueing and backoff patterns that keep throughput stable under 429s.
- [OpenRouter Alternatives: A Buyer's Checklist](https://runixcloud.io/blog/openrouter-alternatives) — Evaluating LLM gateways beyond routing: the contract, data, failover and cost-attribution questions that decide whether a gateway survives procurement.
- [Prompt Caching: When It Pays and When It Bites](https://runixcloud.io/blog/prompt-caching-explained) — How provider-side prompt caching works, the prefix rule that decides whether you get hits, and the cases where caching quietly changes behaviour.
- [Streaming LLM Responses Without Breaking Failover](https://runixcloud.io/blog/streaming-llm-failover) — Once tokens have reached the user, failover stops being free. Mid-stream failure modes, what a proxy must preserve, and how to degrade without duplicating text.
- [What Is an LLM Gateway? A Plain Definition](https://runixcloud.io/blog/what-is-an-llm-gateway) — An LLM gateway is a control plane between your application and model providers. What it does, what it does not do, and when a team actually needs one.
- [LLM Cost Control: Tokens, Caching, and Budgets Explained](https://runixcloud.io/blog/llm-cost-control) — Token pricing asymmetry, prompt caching, model routing, budgets and kill switches — and the waste patterns that quietly inflate an LLM bill.
- [From Raw to Model-Ready: A Practical Guide to AI Data Pipelines](https://runixcloud.io/blog/ai-data-pipelines) — A stage-by-stage guide to AI data pipelines: ingestion, cleaning, deduplication, LLM-powered extraction, PII masking and quality scoring.
- [Designing for Model Failover: Lessons from Production LLM Traffic](https://runixcloud.io/blog/model-failover) — Keeping LLM-backed products up when providers degrade: failure taxonomy, retry budgets, circuit breakers, failover trade-offs and degradation tiers.
- [Choosing an LLM Gateway: Seven Things That Actually Matter](https://runixcloud.io/blog/llm-gateway-guide) — How to evaluate an LLM gateway: API compatibility, failover behaviour, rate limits, cost tracking, observability, security and operational burden.
- [Introducing Runix](https://runixcloud.io/blog/introducing-runix) — Why we started Runix and what we set out to build: the gateway now called Runix Router, the pipelines now Runix Pipeline and Runix Data, and what came next.
